unit_title: Unit 4: Indigenous Knowledge - Comprehensive Master Guide on Direct & Indirect Speech
content: Unit 4: Grammar Focus - Exhaustive Master Guide on Direct and Indirect (Reported) Speech (Communicative English Skills II - EnLa102) ========================================= 1. CORE CONCEPTS AND FUNDAMENTALS ========================================= What is Direct and Indirect (Reported) Speech? In English grammar, we use two primary methods to report spoken or written communication: Direct Speech (ቀጥተኛ ንግግር) and Indirect / Reported Speech (እርምጃ/ዘገባዊ ንግግር)። • Direct Speech (ቀጥተኛ ንግግር): Reproduces the exact words spoken by a person inside quotation marks ("..."). Example: Kebede said, "I am researching indigenous herbal medicine today." • Indirect / Reported Speech (ዘገባዊ ንግግር): Relays the substance of what was said without quoting exact words. It removes quotation marks, adjusts pronouns, backshifts tenses (when the reporting verb is in the past), and alters time/place adverbs. Example: Kebede said that he was researching indigenous herbal medicine that day. ========================================= 2. DETAILED RULE BREAKDOWN BY SENTENCE TYPES ========================================= CATEGORY A: STATEMENTS / DECLARATIVE SENTENCES (Affirmative & Negative) 1. Conjunction Usage: Use the conjunction that to introduce the reported clause (optional in informal speech, mandatory in academic writing). 2. Reporting Verb Selection: • Use say (that) when no direct listener is mentioned. • Use tell + personal object (me/him/her/us/them/Betru) + that when a listener is specified. • Use academic alternatives: stated, explained, claimed, argued, mentioned, added, asserted, pointed out. Direct: Birhane said, "Indigenous knowledge solves environmental problems." Indirect: Birhane stated that indigenous knowledge solved environmental problems. Direct: She said to me, "I don't agree with external solutions." Indirect: She told me that she didn't agree with external solutions. ─────────────────────────── CATEGORY B: QUESTIONS / INTERROGATIVE SENTENCES When reporting questions, NEVER use question word order (Verb + Subject). Always convert the question into statement word order (Subject + Verb) and remove the question mark (?). 1. Wh- Questions (who, what, where, when, why, how): • Retain the Wh- word as the connecting conjunction. • Change order from `Wh- word + Auxiliary + Subject + Main Verb` to `Wh- word + Subject + Backshifted Verb`. • Remove auxiliary verbs do, does, did. Direct: "Where did you find this traditional remedy?" the doctor asked. Indirect: The doctor asked where I had found that traditional remedy. 2. Yes/No Questions (starting with Is, Are, Do, Does, Did, Have, Can, Will): • Introduce the reported clause using if or whether. • Change order to `if/whether + Subject + Backshifted Verb`. Direct: "Do local farmers use crop rotation?" the scholar asked. Indirect: The scholar asked if local farmers used crop rotation. ─────────────────────────── CATEGORY C: IMPERATIVES (Commands, Requests, Orders, Advice, Warnings) Imperatives do not undergo tense backshifting. Instead, they transform into Infinitive Structures (To + Verb 1) or Negative Infinitives (Not to + Verb 1). 1. Positive Imperative Rules: • Change the reporting verb to tell, order, ask, advise, command, urge, instruct + personal object + to + V1. Direct: "Preserve your native traditions," the elder said to us. Indirect: The elder urged us to preserve our native traditions. 2. Negative Imperative Rules: • Place not BEFORE the infinitive: not to + V1. • CRITICAL TRAP: Writing "to not + V1" is grammatically incorrect in reported speech. Direct: "Don't ignore community practices," the teacher said. Indirect: The teacher advised us not to ignore community practices. ─────────────────────────── CATEGORY D: SPECIAL REPORTING VERB STRUCTURES (Infinitives & Gerunds) Many advanced reporting verbs take specific syntactic structures instead of a standard standard `that`-clause: 1. Verb + To-Infinitive (offer, promise, agree, refuse, threaten, claim): • Direct: "I will document the oral history," Chala said. • Indirect: Chala promised to document the oral history. 2. Verb + Object + To-Infinitive (advise, allow, invite, remind, warn): • Direct: "You should read Mkapa's essay," Aster told me. • Indirect: Aster advised me to read Mkapa's essay. 3. Verb + Gerund / -ing (suggest, recommend, admit, deny, regret): • Direct: "Let's consult the local healers," Tigist said. • Indirect: Tigist suggested consulting the local healers. • Alternative: Tigist suggested that we (should) consult the local healers. 4. Verb + Preposition + Gerund (apologize for, insist on, accuse of, congratulate on): • Direct: "I am sorry for missing the presentation," Dawit said. • Indirect: Dawit apologized for missing the presentation. ─────────────────────────── CATEGORY E: EXCLAMATIONS AND OPTATIVE/WISH SENTENCES • Exclamations: Use reporting verbs like exclaimed with joy/sorrow/surprise or convert to statement. Direct: "What a sustainable method this is!" the researcher said. Indirect: The researcher exclaimed with admiration that that method was very sustainable. • Wishes / Greetings: Use wished, prayed, greeted. Direct: "Good luck on your exam," she said to me. Indirect: She wished me good luck on my exam. ========================================= 3. EXHAUSTIVE TRANSFORMATION MATRICES ========================================= A. Complete 12-Tense Backshifting Matrix • Simple Present → Simple Past Direct: "Farmers know the soil conditions," he said. Indirect: He said that farmers knew the soil conditions. • Present Continuous → Past Continuous Direct: "We are studying local practices," she said. Indirect: She said that they were studying local practices. • Present Perfect → Past Perfect Direct: "They have protected the forest for centuries," he said. Indirect: He said that they had protected the forest for centuries. • Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous Direct: "I have been working on this project," Sara said. Indirect: Sara said that she had been working on that project. • Simple Past → Past Perfect Direct: "The community built this terrace system long ago," he noted. Indirect: He noted that the community had built that terrace system long before. • Past Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous Direct: "The elders were explaining the customary law," Almaz said. Indirect: Almaz said that the elders had been explaining the customary law. • Past Perfect → Past Perfect (UNCHANGED) Direct: "Scientists had ignored local wisdom," he stated. Indirect: He stated that scientists had ignored local wisdom. • Past Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous (UNCHANGED) Direct: "We had been living in harmony with nature," they said. Indirect: They said that they had been living in harmony with nature. • Future Simple (will) → Conditional (would) Direct: "Modern technology will assist agriculture," she said. Indirect: She said that modern technology would assist agriculture. • Future Continuous (will be -ing) → Conditional Continuous (would be -ing) Direct: "I will be attending the lecture at ten," Solomon said. Indirect: Solomon said that he would be attending the lecture at ten. • Future Perfect (will have + V3) → Conditional Perfect (would have + V3) Direct: "By next year, we will have completed the archive," she said. Indirect: She said that by the following year, they would have completed the archive. ─────────────────────────── B. Modal & Semi-Modal Transformations • Can → Could: Direct: "I can speak Amharic," he said. → Indirect: He said he could speak Amharic. • May → Might: Direct: "It may rain tomorrow," she said. → Indirect: She said it might rain the next day. • Must → Had to (Obligation): Direct: "We must respect elders," he said. → Indirect: He said they had to respect elders. • Must → Must (Permanent truth / Logical deduction): Direct: "Plants must have water," he said. → Indirect: He said that plants must have water. • Shall → Should (Advice) / Would (Future): Direct: "What shall we do?" → Indirect: He asked what they should do. • Have to / Has to → Had to: Direct: "I have to leave," he said. → Indirect: He said he had to leave. • Needn't → Didn't have to / Needn't: Direct: "You needn't worry," she said. → Indirect: She said I didn't have to worry. • Unchanged Modals: Could, Should, Would, Might, Ought to, Used to remain unchanged. ─────────────────────────── C. The SON Pronoun Shift Rule To avoid errors in pronoun transformations, use the S-O-N formula: • 1 (First Person Pronouns - I, we, my, our): Change according to the Subject of the reporting clause. • 2 (Second Person Pronouns - you, your): Change according to the Object of the reporting clause. • 3 (Third Person Pronouns - he, she, it, they, his, her, their): No change. ─────────────────────────── D. Exhaustive Time & Place Adverb Shifts • now → then / at that moment • today → that day • tonight → that night • tomorrow → the next day / the following day • yesterday → the day before / the previous day • next week/month/year → the following week/month/year • last week/month/year → the previous week/month/year / the week before • days ago → days before / earlier • here → there • this / these → that / those • hence → thence ========================================= 4. EXCEPTIONS & SPECIAL CASES (WHEN NOT TO BACKSHIFT) ========================================= 1. Present / Future Reporting Verbs: If the reporting verb is in the Simple Present (says, tells), Present Perfect (has said), or Future Simple (will say), DO NOT change the verb tense inside the reported clause. • Direct: Aster says, "I love studying indigenous wisdom." • Indirect: Aster says that she loves studying indigenous wisdom. 2. Universal Scientific Facts & Permanent General Truths: If the statement expresses an unchanging physical fact or general law of nature, keep the present tense even when reported in the past. • Direct: The instructor stated, "The earth revolves around the sun." • Indirect: The instructor stated that the earth revolves around the sun. 3. Conditionals Type 2 & Type 3: Unreal conditional structures remain unchanged in reported speech. • Direct: "If I had time, I would write a book," Taye said. • Indirect: Taye said that if he had time, he would write a book. (Unchanged) ========================================= 5. COMPREHENSIVE PITFALL & EXAM TRICK MATRIX ========================================= TRICK 1: Word Order Trap in Wh- Questions ❌ INCORRECT: He asked me where did I live in Gondar. ✅ CORRECT: He asked me where I lived in Gondar. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Exams often place auxiliary verbs (did, was, is) before the subject. Always re-arrange to `Subject + Verb` and drop `did/does/do`! TRICK 2: Negative Imperative Word Order Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The doctor ordered the patient to not take the medicine without advice. ✅ CORRECT: The doctor ordered the patient not to take the medicine without advice. 💡 EXAM TRICK: "Not" MUST come before "to". Remember: NOT TO, never TO NOT! TRICK 3: Reporting Verb Misuse ('Say' vs 'Tell') ❌ INCORRECT: Abebe told that he was working offline. ❌ INCORRECT: Abebe said me that he was working offline. ✅ CORRECT: Abebe told me that he was working offline. ✅ CORRECT: Abebe said that he was working offline. 💡 EXAM TRICK: `Tell` requires an object (tell someone). `Say` does not take a direct object without `to` (say that / say to someone). TRICK 4: Present Reporting Verb Backshift Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The professor claims that local remedies were ineffective. ✅ CORRECT: The professor claims that local remedies are ineffective. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Check the reporting verb first! If it ends in `-s` or `-es` (says, claims, asserts), DO NOT change the main clause verb tense! TRICK 5: Double Reporting / Double Auxiliary Trap in Yes/No Questions ❌ INCORRECT: She asked if did I know the answer. ✅ CORRECT: She asked if I knew the answer. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Never keep auxiliary did/do/does when converting Yes/No questions with `if` or `whether`! TRICK 6: Misplacing Time Adverbs ❌ INCORRECT: She said she would visit us tomorrow. ✅ CORRECT: She said she would visit us the next day / the following day. 💡 EXAM TRICK: When reporting past conversations, always convert time adverbs like tomorrow → the next day, today → that day, and yesterday → the day before. ========================================= 6. EXTENDED PRACTICE EXAM QUESTIONS WITH DETAILED RATIONALE ========================================= Question 1: Direct Speech: "Why didn't you attend the meeting yesterday?" The manager asked Kebede ________. A. why didn't he attend the meeting the day before B. why he had not attended the meeting the previous day C. why he didn't attend the meeting yesterday D. why had he not attended the meeting the day before Correct Answer: B. why he had not attended the meeting the previous day Analysis / Rationale: Simple past negative ("didn't attend") backshifts to past perfect negative ("had not attended"). The question word order turns into statement order (Subject 'he' before verb 'had not attended'), and 'yesterday' shifts to 'the previous day'. Question 2: Select the sentence that is grammatically CORRECT: A. Aster suggested to go to the historical site. B. Aster suggested that we should go to the historical site. C. Aster suggested us to go to the historical site. D. Aster suggested we to go to the historical site. Correct Answer: B. Aster suggested that we should go to the historical site. Analysis / Rationale: The reporting verb 'suggest' CANNOT be followed by `object + to-infinitive`. It must be followed by a gerund (`suggest going`) or a `that`-clause with `should` (`suggest that we should go`). Question 3: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT reported sentence: A. The instructor said that light travels in a straight line. B. She requested the students not to make noise during the exam. C. He told that he had finished his research project. D. She asked whether I had seen her notebook. Correct Answer: C. He told that he had finished his research project. Analysis / Rationale: 'Told' requires an indirect personal object (e.g., 'told me' or 'told us'). Using 'told that' without a personal object is incorrect.
